Vaccine Myths vs Facts
A quick, reassuring guide separating common vaccine rumours from the facts.
1. Myth: Vaccines cause autism.
Fact: This myth traces back to a single 1998 study that was later found to be seriously flawed and was retracted by the journal that published it. Since then, many large, independent studies across different countries have found no link between vaccines and autism. Health authorities worldwide, including the WHO, continue to affirm that vaccines are safe on this front.
2. Myth: Natural immunity from catching a disease is better than immunity from a vaccine.
Fact: Vaccines train the immune system to recognise and fight a disease without exposing a person to the actual risks of that illness, such as severe complications or death. Diseases like measles, polio, and rubella can cause serious harm or lifelong disability if caught naturally. Getting immunity through vaccination offers similar protection in a much safer way.
3. Myth: Giving several vaccines at the same visit overloads or weakens a child's immune system.
Fact: A child's immune system deals with far more germs from everyday life, like a common cold, than it does from a combined set of vaccines. Receiving multiple vaccines together has not been shown to cause any negative effect on the body's defences. It also means fewer clinic visits and a better chance of completing the full schedule on time.
4. Myth: Vaccine side effects are usually dangerous.
Fact: Most people who get a vaccine experience only mild, short-lived effects, such as soreness at the injection site, slight fever, or tiredness, which typically go away within a day or two on their own. Serious reactions are extremely rare and are closely monitored by health authorities even after a vaccine is approved. Vaccines undergo rigorous testing before being introduced and continued safety monitoring afterward.
5. Myth: Diseases like measles and polio are basically gone, so vaccination isn't necessary anymore.
Fact: These diseases became rare specifically because sustained, high vaccination coverage kept them under control, not because the germs disappeared. When vaccination rates drop in a community, these diseases can and do return quickly, as seen in real outbreaks in various parts of the world. Continuing to vaccinate is what keeps these illnesses from making a comeback.
6. Myth: Vaccines contain harmful chemicals that poison the body.
Fact: Vaccines do contain small amounts of ingredients like preservatives or adjuvants, but these are present in carefully studied, safe quantities and serve a purpose, such as keeping the vaccine sterile or improving how well it works. These ingredients have been extensively researched and are regularly reviewed by health and drug regulatory bodies. The amounts used are far too small to cause the harm that circulating rumours often suggest.
7. Myth: Vaccines can give you the disease they're meant to prevent.
Fact: Most vaccines use inactivated (killed) or partial versions of a germ, which cannot cause the disease itself. A few vaccines use a weakened live form of a germ, which in most people simply triggers a mild, harmless immune response rather than the actual illness. Any mild symptoms that occasionally follow vaccination, like slight fever, are a sign the body is building protection, not a sign of infection.
8. Myth: Vaccines affect fertility and cause infertility later in life.
Fact: There is no credible scientific evidence linking any routine vaccine to infertility in men or women. This particular myth has circulated widely on social media in various forms over the years and has been investigated and repeatedly disproven by health researchers and public health bodies. Vaccines are studied specifically for their effects on reproductive health as part of standard safety evaluation.
9. Myth: If most people around me are vaccinated, I don't need to get vaccinated myself.
Fact: Community protection, often called herd immunity, only works when enough individuals are vaccinated, and it isn't a guarantee for any one unvaccinated person. Relying on others being vaccinated still leaves you personally at risk of catching the disease, especially while travelling or during local outbreaks. Getting vaccinated protects you directly, in addition to helping protect those around you who may be too young or medically unable to be vaccinated themselves.
Sources
World Health Organization (WHO)
Pan American Health Organization (PAHO/WHO)
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India
Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
National Health Mission (NHM)
UNICEF India
This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
